newsitem.title: USA: Congress passes securities reform bill.
newsitem.headline: Congress passes securities reform bill.

text.p: Congress Tuesday passed a major securities bill to overhaul regulation of mutual funds and give the Securities and Exchange Commission $20 million in additional funds to supervise investment advisers.
The Senate sent the bill to President Bill Clinton on a voice vote after House approval Saturday. Clinton was expected to sign it.

The bill would exempt from state regulation securities offered by mutual funds and stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange, American Stock Exchange, Nasdaq and other exchanges identified by the SEC as providing comparable listing standards.

It would establish an electronic database for disciplinary records of investment advisory funds and advisers that can be checked by individual investors through a toll-free telephone number. The bill called for state regulation of the nation's 150,000 investment advisers while the SEC oversees firms.

The bill, endorsed by the SEC, would also cut fees that public corporations pay for routine filings with the SEC by $850 million over 10 years and let brokerage firms borrow from financial institutions besides banks.
Sponsors of the bill called it the first major overhaul of securities law in 50 years and said it would promote efficiency in capital markets.
"This bill represents a triumph of reason and moderation over extremism and ideology," Representative Ed Markey, D-Mass., said.

"The bill strikes a proper balance by eliminating overlapping state and federal regulation, yet without undermining investor protection," said Mark Griffin, president of the North American Securitiies Administrators Association.
Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, R-N.Y., said the bill created "a truly national mutual fund marketplace with uniform standards that will benefit investors and consumers."

SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt said in a statement that, "Without compromising investor protection, this important legislation will eliminate regulatory overlap between the states and federal government, and will significantly restructure the way mutual funds and coprorate securities are regulated."
State regulators, meanwhile, said the legislation called on states to accept "significant responsibilities and changes," particularly regarding the regulation of investment advisers.

Mark Griffin, president of the North American Securities Admninistrators Asociation, which groups state regulatory chiefs, said the legislation should speed passage of investment advisory regulations in four states: Ohio, Iowa, Colorado and Wyoming.
He said state regulators will work with state governors and consumer groups to improve regulation at the state level aimed at helping investors.

The Securities Industry Association, which represents the largest brokerage houses in the nation, said the reforms Congress aprpoved "will clear away some of the regulatory underbrush that adds to the cost of capital, without compromising investor protections."
